hero_lead: PositionTracker shows participants of running and cycling races on a map, with standings, gaps and an expected finish time. Spectators open a link in the browser. Participants need a phone with the free OwnTracks app. The organizer sees positions without delay.
demo_note: The demo runs in your browser with made-up riders and a made-up course. It is a simplified simulation: no server, no real GPS. The organizer view shows everything instantly, including alarms and battery level. The spectator view is delayed by 15 s, has no alarms and hides the names of those who did not agree. The star next to a rider follows them: the map zooms to them and the others shrink. Select a rider and try "Stops".
who_h: Four roles and what the app gives each
w1_p: Family and friends see on the map where you are, with the delay the organizer set (5 to 300 seconds). They do not have to ask at the finish whether you have arrived.
w1_a: A phone in a jersey pocket is enough. No separate GPS tracker.
w1_b: Spectators see an expected finish time. It is an estimate from your recent speed.
w1_c: Your number and nickname appear in the public standings, if you want.
w2_p: The app shows pace in min/km, the gap to the runner ahead and an expected finish time. The estimate has a range of at least one minute.
w2_a: Pace in min/km instead of km/h, automatically by sport.
w2_b: Below 20 % battery the organizer gets an alert, as long as the phone reports its battery level.
w2_c: Once the organizer ends the event, the server no longer accepts positions. Positions are deleted 30 days after the end.
w3_p: Map, standings, coloured sectors and alarms for a stopped rider, a rider off the course, lost signal and low battery. Alarms work only while the phone is sending positions.
w3_a: Email invitations in Slovak and English, reminders with one click.
w3_b: GPX course, laps, checkpoints, categories and start waves.
w3_c: A public link for spectators with an adjustable delay.
w4_p: No installation, no account. You open the link, find your favourite and watch them approach the finish.
w4_a: A star next to a name: the map zooms to your rider and shrinks the others.
w4_b: An alert on the page when your rider crosses the finish line (while the page is open).
w4_c: Share a rider with one tap.

sc1_alt: Race control: map, standings and messages
sc1_p: A map with all riders, standings with coloured sectors, messages about stopped riders, riders off the course, lost signal and low battery.
sc2_p: The biggest figure is the ETA to the finish. Below it distance, speed and sectors.
sc3_p: The page follows the device setting. The toggle is always at hand.
sc4_p: Who confirmed and who did not. Resend, remind and re-issue the link with one click.

sc6_p: Upload a GPX, set laps, checkpoints, categories and the spectator delay.
g_lead: Pick your role. The steps match what you will see in the app.
o0_h: Prepare the course as a GPX file
o0_p: No GPS knowledge is needed. The free tool gpx.studio is enough: it runs in the browser, needs no account, and you draw the course by clicking on the map. If you already have the route in Strava, Komoot, Garmin Connect or on Mapy.com, just download it from there as GPX and skip this step.
o0_1: Open gpx.studio/app. Use the magnifier on the right to find the place of the race and zoom in until you can see individual streets. From too far away the tool cannot draw a route ("start point is too far from the nearest road").
o0_2: On the left choose the tool Plan or edit a route (the pencil icon). Keep Routing switched on in the panel and pick the sport under Activity (bike or run): the route then snaps to roads that suit the sport.
o0_3: Click the map in the order the race will go. Every click adds a point and the tool joins it to the previous one along the road. You can drag a point elsewhere if you do not like the route.
o0_4: For a loop press Back to start at the end: the last point is joined to the start. If the route runs the wrong way round, use Reverse.
o0_5: Check the length at the bottom left (with several laps it is the length of one lap).
o0_6: At the top choose File → Export… (or Ctrl+S) and in the Export options window press Download file. A file ending in .gpx is downloaded.
o0_fig1_p: Five clicks on the map and "Back to start". Bottom left you see the length of the route (5.67 km) and the elevation profile. The circles are the points you clicked.
o0_fig2_p: File → Export… opens a window, press "Download file" in it. Leave the "OpenStreetMap data" checkbox empty.
o0_dl: Want to try the procedure? Download the sample GPX file made exactly from this example (a loop through Žilina, 5.67 km, 162 points) and upload it in the application when you create an event.
o0_tip: What the application requires of the file: at least 50 m per lap, up to 1 MB, and for several laps a loop whose end is at most 100 m from the start. That is why you use "Back to start" for a loop. You do not mark a start line: the start is the first point of the course.
q7: I do not know how to create a GPX file. What now?
a7: Draw the course by clicking on the map in the free tool gpx.studio and export it (File → Export…). The exact steps are in the organizer guide, first step.
o1_p: Enter your name and email. There is no password: you sign in with a one-time link sent by email. Open the link and press "Confirm email". Only then can you upload a course and invite participants (abuse protection).
o2_h: Create the event and upload the course
o2_p: Name, place, start date and time, sport. Then a GPX file, the number of laps (1 to 10), checkpoints and the spectator delay (5 to 300 seconds). A course with several laps must be closed.
o2_tip: Tip: the default delay is 30 seconds. A shorter delay gives a more current picture, a longer one makes it harder to read rivals' tactics from the standings.
o3_p: Name, email, gender, email language, category, wave. The bib is assigned automatically, or you enter it. The invitation goes out immediately. The list shows Invited, Confirmed, Declined and Email failed, and you can send a reminder, resend, or issue a new link.
o3_tip: Spectators see a participant's name only with consent. For minors only the bib is shown publicly.
o4_p: Press "Mark as ready" and on race day "Go live". The app shows the public link for spectators: post it and put it on posters as a QR code. Once live, the course can no longer be changed.
o5_p: The "Race control" tab shows the map, standings, sectors and messages. Press "Acknowledge" to handle an alarm, find the rider on the map, and mark a rider who has withdrawn as DNF. Unhandled messages stay on top, handled ones are dimmed.
o6_p: Press "Finish event". Positions are deleted after 30 days by themselves. If a participant asks, you delete their data immediately (only the bib remains). You issue the official results: read the spectator standings as indicative.
p0_p: There is no PositionTracker app for participants. Your position during the race is sent by OwnTracks, a free open-source app you install once. It runs in the background, so you can leave the phone locked in your pocket.
p0_tip: A phone without Google Play? The app is also on F-Droid. Look for exactly "OwnTracks" (developer OwnTracks), not similar-sounding apps. Do not set anything up when you first open the app: you get the configuration from your invitation in step 4.
p1_p: In the organizer's email click your personal link. The page appears in your language and shows the event, your name and bib. Confirm (or decline) and, if you like, choose a nickname (max. 30 characters).
p2_p: Consent to share your location during the race is required. The organizer sees you exactly, spectators with a delay. Optionally allow showing your name (otherwise they see only the bib). The data is deleted after 30 days.
p3_p: On the phone with OwnTracks installed tap "Set up OwnTracks", or scan the QR code from another device, and accept the import. Nothing is typed by hand.
p3_tip: The setup contains your device's secret key. Do not share it. If you lost it, repeat the consent: the old key stops working.
p4_p: Android: Settings → Apps → OwnTracks → Battery → Unrestricted; Location → Allow all the time. iPhone: Settings → OwnTracks → Location → Always, Precise Location on, Background App Refresh on. Keep the app in "Move" mode.
p5_h: At the start and during the race
p5_p: Before the start check that the app shows no error after sending a position. Do not switch the phone off or turn on battery saver. SOS is not a button in the app: phone the organizer. The organizer marks a withdrawal.
s1_p: The organizer sends you a link or a QR code. No installation, no account. At the top a notice says positions are delayed: the standings are indicative.
s2_p: Search by name or bib, filter by category. The star next to a name follows them: the map zooms to your rider and the other riders shrink.
s3_p: The biggest figure is the expected finish time and its range. Below it distance covered, speed (or pace), rank and gap, and coloured sectors: purple is the fastest sector of everyone, green your best, yellow slower.
s4_p: Turn on "Notify me at the finish" and the page alerts you when the rider crosses the line (while it stays open). "Share" sends a link straight to your rider.
f1: apps for spectators. A link in the browser is enough.
f2: free app for the participant: OwnTracks. It runs in the background if you allow location and remove the battery restriction.
f3: after the event ends, the positions delete themselves. Spectators see a name only with consent, and never a minor's.
f4: spectator delay is yours to set; the organizer sees everything instantly.
q1: Do I need my own GPS tracker?
a1: No. A phone in a jersey pocket, backpack or armband is enough. The free OwnTracks app sends the position in the background if you allow location and battery use (participant guide, step 4).
a2: OwnTracks sends unsent positions when the connection returns. After 2 minutes without a new position the rider is marked "offline", and both the organizer and spectators see it. Behaviour in long outages is still being verified in the field.
q3: Can spectators see my exact position?
a3: No. Spectators see your position with a delay of 5 to 300 seconds, set by the organizer. Only the organizer sees it without delay.
q4: Does it work for running and cycling?
a4: Yes. For running the app shows pace in min/km, for cycling km/h. The OwnTracks configuration differs by sport: a position every 5 s when cycling, every 10 s when running.
q5: Where does it run and what state is it in?
a5: PositionTracker is an MVP for now, not a full-featured application. It runs in Docker with PostgreSQL, so you can run it on your own server. The deployment guide is in the repository.
a6: No. Spectator standings are indicative because positions are delayed. The organizer issues the official results.
fin_h: Try it on your own event
fin_p: Switch the demo to the spectator view and compare it with the organizer view. Then you can create your own event.
fin_app: Create an account and start your race

foot_cookies: Only settings you chose, no cookies, no tracking.
what_p: PositionTracker is a web service for tracking the position of participants in running and cycling races in near real time on a map. The organizer creates an event, uploads the course as a GPX file and invites participants by email. Participants send their position from the phone with the OwnTracks app (Android, iPhone). Spectators follow the standings, gaps and the expected finish time through a public link, without an account and without installing anything.
spec1_d: Running and cycling; a loop with several laps or a single lap
spec2_d: A web browser; sign-in by a one-time link sent by email, no password
spec3_d: The free OwnTracks app for Android and iPhone
spec4_d: A public link in the browser; positions delayed by 5 to 300 seconds as set by the organizer
spec6_d: Positions are deleted 30 days after the event ends; spectators see a name only with consent

story_p1: My colleague Qto is a passionate cyclist and a man who knows his way around vibration and signal measurement: he can spot one bad bearing in a chart at a glance. Over a beer he told me he struggles to give an AI its work. The problem was not the AI. It was what you ask of it and how.
story_p2: An AI is not a calibrated sensor, it is a capable new colleague. Sceptics are right that you should not trust it blindly: you have to steer it and check its work. Tell it "just do something" and you get something. PositionTracker came out of a method: a specification (what I want, what it runs on, how I will check it), implementation with AI, verification, deployment. It is proof of the method, not proof that AI is a miracle. And it is an MVP, not a full-featured application.
